title: Independence Bias in Meta-Analyses of Paired Anatomic Data
content: Marginal prevalences of paired binary outcomes generally do not identify their joint prevalence. Reconstructing bilateral anatomical prevalence by multiplying left- and right-side prevalences therefore imposes an unverified dependence assumption. We define Independence Bias as the signed difference between this reconstruction and the true joint prevalence, and derive sharp study-specific and pooled bounds. Under nonnegative association, maximum underestimation equals the smaller marginal prevalence minus their product, with a global maximum of 0.25 at equal marginals of 0.5. Allowing negative association requires both Fréchet endpoints. For a pooled prevalence with fixed nonnegative weights, maximum underestimation is the weighted mean of study-specific bounds. We also establish the midpoint reconstruction’s minimax property, distinguish anatomical endpoints, accommodate studies with observed joint outcomes, and construct a conservative confidence interval for the pooled bound from marginal binomial counts. A hypothetical three-study meta-analysis illustrates estimation of the maximum possible pooled underestimation and quantification of sampling uncertainty in this bound. These results separate unidentified dependence from sampling uncertainty and provide a reproducible sensitivity framework for anatomical evidence synthesis. Re-estimated weights and transformed-scale meta-analyses require separate model-based sensitivity analyses.
